flashcards.q: What is NAPI and why does it exist?
flashcards.a: New API: after the first hardIRQ on packet arrival, the driver switches to polling mode (softirq context, default budget 64 packets/pass) instead of interrupting per-packet, preventing a receive livelock under high packet rates.

flashcards.q: What does interrupt coalescing trade off?
flashcards.a: ethtool -c settings (rx-usecs/rx-frames) delay the hardware interrupt to batch more packets per interrupt, reducing CPU overhead under sustained load at the cost of added per-packet latency and jitter.
Generic Receive Offload: coalesces multiple physically-received TCP segments of the same stream into one larger skb before IP/TCP processing, amortizing per-segment processing cost.

flashcards.q: How many round trips does a TLS 1.3 handshake need versus TLS 1.2?
flashcards.a: TLS 1.3: 1 RTT (client sends key share speculatively in the first flight). TLS 1.2: 2 RTT. 0-RTT resumption can send app data in the first flight but with no replay protection.

flashcards.q: What is the catch with TLS 0-RTT resumption?
flashcards.a: The first flight of 0-RTT application data has no replay protection -- an attacker can capture and resend it, so production restricts 0-RTT to idempotent requests (GET) or disables it for side-effecting endpoints.

flashcards.q: Why do browsers open 6-8 parallel connections per origin under HTTP/1.1?
flashcards.a: HTTP/1.1 allows only one request in flight per connection in practice (pipelining is unused due to HOL blocking and broken proxies), so browsers parallelize connections instead -- each paying its own TCP+TLS handshake.

flashcards.q: What causes TCP-level head-of-line blocking in HTTP/2?
flashcards.a: TCP guarantees strict in-order delivery for the whole connection as one byte stream; a lost packet for one multiplexed stream blocks delivery of all later-arrived bytes, including unrelated streams, until it's retransmitted.

flashcards.q: How does QUIC/HTTP-3 fix TCP head-of-line blocking?
flashcards.a: QUIC implements its own reliability with independent per-stream loss recovery over UDP, so a lost packet only stalls its own stream; other streams' already-arrived data is delivered immediately.

flashcards.q: Why can QUIC survive a client IP change (WiFi to cellular) but TCP can't?
flashcards.a: TCP identifies a connection by the 4-tuple (src/dst IP:port), which breaks on an IP change. QUIC identifies a connection by a connection ID independent of IP address.

flashcards.q: What is the real tradeoff of QUIC/HTTP-3 versus TCP that keeps it from being a strict upgrade?
flashcards.a: QUIC's userspace reliability implementation currently costs more server-side CPU per byte than TCP's decades-optimized, often hardware-offloaded kernel path -- a real, unresolved cost for CPU-bound, low-loss internal services.

flashcards.q: How does HPACK header compression differ from gzipping headers?
flashcards.a: HPACK maintains a stateful shared dynamic table across the connection's lifetime so repeated headers are referenced by a short index instead of resent; stateless per-message gzip can't exploit that cross-request redundancy and was avoided partly because it enabled CRIME/BREACH-style compression side-channel attacks.

flashcards.q: What does curl -w's per-phase timing let you attribute latency to?
flashcards.a: DNS resolution (time_namelookup), TCP connect (time_connect), TLS handshake (time_appconnect), and time-to-first-byte (time_starttransfer) -- pinpointing which layer actually added latency instead of guessing.

flashcards.q: What does a cold DNS resolution cost versus a cached one?
flashcards.a: Cached: effectively 0 extra RTT. Cold recursive resolution (root -> TLD -> authoritative) commonly adds tens of milliseconds.
